01
The Problem
مسئلہ

A Class 10 student in Sahiwal is handed two documents each year. A syllabus, which lists what to learn. And a pairing scheme — the board's own published breakdown of which chapters get paired into which questions, and how many marks each is worth.

Nobody hands them the third thing. A plan.

That gap is the entire problem. The student knows what to study and roughly where the marks are — but turning that into "what do I do today, for four months, across eight subjects" is a scheduling problem most adults would struggle with. So it gets solved the only way it can be: badly, at 2 a.m., a week before the paper.

Why the obvious solutions don't reach them

Foreign study apps

Built for SAT, A-Levels or generic "productivity". They have never heard of the Punjab Board, PCTB textbooks, or a pairing scheme. A timetable that treats every chapter as equally important is actively misleading here.

AI chatbots

Excellent at answering a question. Useless at owning a four-month plan. Ask one to build your schedule and it invents a plausible-looking timetable with no grounding in what the board actually rewards.

That leaves the two options students actually fall back on. Private tuition works — and is gated by money, so the students who can least afford an academy are the ones who most need the structure one provides. Paper timetables are free, and are abandoned by week two, because they cannot absorb a missed day, a sick week, or the discovery that Chemistry is harder than expected.

The four constraints that shaped every decision

Building for this student is not building for a Silicon Valley user with a flagship phone and fibre broadband. Four realities shaped the architecture:

Load-shedding Power cuts are routine. A study tool that needs a live connection is a study tool that fails on the evenings the student finally had time.
Mobile data costs money Every megabyte is a decision. An app that streams or re-downloads constantly is an app that gets uninstalled.
Budget Android phones Modest CPUs, limited storage. Heavy frameworks and constant background work are not affordable.
No account, no barrier Requiring a signup before a student can see any value loses most of them at the first screen.
The design consequence

Manzil is offline-first, not offline-capable. Every screen works with no internet and no account. The only network traffic in the entire app is the AI features, plus cloud backup — and cloud backup is strictly optional. Onboarding has no signup step at all.

02
What Manzil Actually Is
حل

Manzil turns the board's own marks distribution into a day-by-day study plan, then keeps that plan alive as real life happens to it.

The study plan is not AI-generated.
That is the single most important design decision in this project.

An AI-generated timetable is a guess dressed as a schedule — untestable, unreproducible, and liable to change its mind between runs. A student's exam preparation is not a reasonable place for that. So the calendar is produced by a deterministic engine: real code, real arithmetic, real board data. Same student, same plan, every time — protected by 989 automated tests that run before every release.

AI is layered on top for what AI is genuinely better at than code: explaining a concept, marking handwriting, generating practice questions, reading a page of notes. The AI teaches. The engine plans.

The moat: data nobody else has bothered to encode

Every chapter in Manzil carries three numbers that most apps do not have and could not fake:

weight (1–5) How heavily the board's pairing scheme actually rewards this chapter. Derived from the official 2026 schemes. This is not a guess about importance — it is the exam's own answer.
difficulty (1–5) How hard this chapter typically is, which changes how much time it deserves relative to its weight.
estMinutes Realistic study time for a first pass, so the schedule reflects effort, not just chapter count.
12
subjects across Science & Arts groups
245
chapter entries (Class 9 + Class 10)
12
boards — all 9 Punjab BISE, plus Federal, Karachi, Peshawar
6
class × group combinations fully covered
How this data was verified

Curriculum data is the one thing in this project that cannot be "mostly right". Every subject and chapter list was cross-checked against multiple independent sources, with an explicit rule that Class 9 and Class 10 follow different curriculum cycles — Class 9 uses the newer national-curriculum books, Class 10 the current PCTB set. A correct-looking source for the wrong year is worse than no source, so anything thin is marked as such in the data rather than shipped as a confident guess.

What the student sees on day one

1
A 60-second setup, with no account

Name, Class 9 or 10, Science or Arts group, board, exam date, and honest confidence ratings per subject. No email, no password, no verification.

2
A complete plan, instantly, offline

Every day between today and the exam is filled — which chapters, which subjects, how many minutes each. Generated on the phone in milliseconds.

3
A plan that survives contact with reality

Miss three days and it re-spreads the work. Study ahead and it lets you — then tells you to rest. Change your available hours and it re-balances without erasing what you have already completed.

03
The Algorithm
نظام

How a syllabus, an exam date and "I can study three hours a day" become a specific instruction for this afternoon.

Stage one — the plan is built in three phases

The runway between today and the exam is divided, not filled uniformly:

Study Pass
Cover every examinable chapter once. Heavier chapters get proportionally more minutes.
→
Revision Cycles
Repeated passes over the same material. Depth scales with the student's own confidence rating.
→
Practice Drills
Past-paper style work, anchored near the exam where it does the most good.

Stage two — how minutes are actually assigned

1
Each chapter earns a time budget

Base estimate, scaled by board weight and difficulty, then adjusted by the student's own confidence. A heavy chapter you're weak at earns far more time than a light one you already know.

2
Chapters are sliced into real study blocks

Blocks tile each day exactly — no dead ten-minute gaps, no 78-minute "focused sessions" nobody sustains. Subjects rotate so no day becomes four hours of one subject.

3
The daily target is a hard ceiling, never a suggestion

If the student said three hours, no day exceeds three hours. This sounds obvious; it is asserted explicitly in the test suite because an earlier version quietly overbooked 101 days out of 224.

4
When time is genuinely too short, it triages by marks

With only days left, not everything fits. Rather than truncating in syllabus order, the engine queues heaviest-weight chapters first — so the chapters that get dropped are the ones worth fewest marks. On a 7-day runway this took heavy-chapter coverage from 17 of 32 chapters to 23 of 32.

The detail that makes it feel human

A student who finishes today's work may pull forward up to three days of future sessions — and then the app stops them and tells them to rest. It also refuses to hand out fresh work to someone who has already completed everything for today. A planner that punishes diligence by endlessly generating more work is a planner students abandon.

Stage three — keeping the plan alive

Every time the student opens the app, the plan is checked and repaired before anything renders. The logic is deliberately careful about one specific case: if nothing is pending today but something was completed today, it does nothing. The student finished their day and earned the rest. Only a genuine hole — nothing done, nothing pending, future work waiting — pulls work forward.

Change your daily hours mid-year and the plan re-spreads rather than regenerating, preserving completed work and readiness. Only switching class or group forces a rebuild — gated behind a confirmation naming exactly how many completed sessions would be lost.

Stage four — turning progress into a predicted grade

Readiness blends coverage (how much of the plan is done) with mastery (quiz performance), weighted by each chapter's board weight — so finishing heavy chapters moves the number more than finishing light ones. That produces a per-subject score, a predicted grade band, and an exam-day risk list: chapters ranked by marks at risk, meaning heavy chapters you have barely touched surface first.

04
The AI Layer
مصنوعی ذہانت

Six AI-powered features, all running through a single layer built to survive a bad network, an exhausted quota and a model that goes down mid-session.

Every request carries Pakistan with it

The most common failure of AI in a local product is that it answers like it has never heard of the place. Ask a generic model about "Chapter 9" and it will happily explain an American textbook.

Manzil prevents this structurally. A context block is injected as a system instruction on every single AI call in the app — not pasted into the user's message, where a student could overwrite it:

// Sent with every request the app makes — quiz, chat, grading, notes.
APP_CONTEXT =
  "This request comes from Manzil, a study-planning app used by
  students in Pakistan preparing for their Matriculation (SSC,
  Class 9-10) board exams under the Punjab Boards of Intermediate
  and Secondary Education (BISE), following the PCTB curriculum.
  Ground every answer in this exact context."

On top of that, the tutor receives the student's own profile — their name, class, group, board, their full subject list for the year, and which subjects they rated themselves weakest in. The result is a tutor that knows a Class 10 Science student in Multan is not a Class 9 Arts student in Peshawar.

Measured, not assumed

Adding this context block costs roughly 60 extra tokens per request, with no measurable latency penalty and no safety-filter interference. It was tested against the live API rather than estimated.

The tutor speaks like a Pakistani teacher

Ustaad's instructions go well beyond "be helpful". They encode how teachers here actually talk:

  • Language mirroring. Urdu script in, Urdu script out. Roman Urdu in, Roman Urdu out. English in, simple English out — with Urdu terms mixed in, because that is how real explanation sounds in a Pakistani classroom.
  • Greeting register matching. A salam earns a salam back. "Hello" earns an everyday greeting — never a salam, because answering "Hello" with "Wa Alaikum Assalam" is subtly wrong, and students notice.
  • No unprompted greetings. If the student just asks a question, the answer starts immediately. No "Great question!" padding.

Built so it does not fall over

Free-tier AI quotas run out and individual models genuinely go down. The app is engineered around both:

Two-axis fallback

Every request has a chain of models and a pool of API keys. If a quota is hit, it rotates to the next key on the same model. If a model is down or times out, it rotates to the next model — because a broken model is broken for every key.

Why it matters: the student never sees a failure that a different key or model could have served.
Ordered by what matters

Text models are ordered by daily quota, so the highest-allowance model is tried first. Vision models are ordered by measured speed — one tier tested ~11× slower on image tasks specifically, so it is tried last, not first.

Result: photo grading returns in ~10 seconds instead of ~114.
Structured output, never guesswork

Anything feeding app logic — quizzes, grades, flashcards — is requested in strict JSON mode with an enforced schema. The app never parses free text hoping the model formatted it correctly.

Result: a malformed AI response cannot corrupt the student's data.
Failure is always explained

Errors are typed — offline, missing key, API failure, unreadable response — and each has its own plain-language message. "No internet" is only ever shown when the failure genuinely looks like lost connectivity.

Result: no AI feature can crash a screen or dead-end a student.
Speed work, all measured on the live API

Reasoning overhead is disabled on the models that support it — dropping one model from 27 seconds to 10. Photos are downscaled to 1568px and re-encoded before upload: visually lossless at the model's own working resolution, but 5–10× smaller, which on Pakistani mobile data is the difference between usable and abandoned. Every request has a timeout so a hung model falls forward instead of freezing the screen.

05
Every Feature
خصوصیات

Fourteen features across five areas. For each: what it does, and the hard problem underneath it.

Intelligence — powered by Gemini

Ustaad — the AI tutor
AI
استاد

A subject tutor that knows the student's exact class, group, board and syllabus. Answers in whichever language the student writes in. Supports voice input — speak a question in Urdu or English instead of typing it, which matters enormously for students who type slowly in either script.

The hard part: making it feel local rather than generic. Solved with the injected context block, the student's profile, and explicit rules for greeting register and language mirroring.
AI Examiner — answer grading
AI
امتحان

The student writes an answer on paper — exactly as they will in the exam — photographs it, and gets it marked like a BISE examiner would: a score, what earned marks, what leaked marks, and a warm one-line note.

The hard part: a 2-mark short answer and a 10-mark long answer are graded completely differently. The examiner is briefed per mark band — at 2 marks it is told explicitly that brevity is correct and asked for fewer improvements, because demanding four faults on a two-line answer forces a model to invent them. Verified live: the same answer scores 2/2 with one suggestion at 2 marks, and 3/10 with four at 10 marks.
Snap-to-Study — notes to flashcards
AI

Photograph a page of handwritten or printed notes; the app extracts the key facts and turns them into review flashcards automatically.

The hard part: upload size on metered data. Images are downscaled and re-encoded first — 5–10× smaller with no loss of legibility to the model.
Adaptive quizzes
AI

Generates board-style questions for any chapter on demand. Results feed directly into the readiness score, so quiz performance changes the predicted grade.

The hard part: reliability. Questions are requested under a strict JSON schema, so a badly-formatted response fails cleanly instead of rendering a broken quiz.

Attention & wellbeing — on-device, no cloud

Focus Guard — attention tracking
On-device AI
توجہ

Uses the front camera and on-device machine learning to detect whether the student is actually present and engaged during a study session — then pauses the timer when they walk away, so a 25-minute session means 25 minutes of study.

The hard part: the design pivot. A student revising from a book looks down at the book, not at the phone — so "eyes on screen" is exactly the wrong signal. Instead it measures presence, orientation relative to the student's own calibrated posture, and stability. That calibration is what makes it work at a desk, on a bed, on the floor, or on a charpai.
Focus Guard voice
Offline

Spoken guidance at the moments the student cannot read the screen — while positioning the phone, after walking away, or when they look sleepy. Five studio-quality voices to choose from.

The hard part: latency and load-shedding. All 105 clips are pre-rendered and bundled into the app rather than generated at runtime — so they play in roughly zero milliseconds, work with no internet, cost no quota, and ship no API key to the phone.
Breathe — stress relief
Offline
سکون

A guided box-breathing exercise with an animated orb, launched straight from the Today screen. Built for the moment before a paper when panic is the actual obstacle.

The hard part: the animation had to stay perfectly in step with the breathing count on slow phones, so the timing runs on a plain clock rather than animation callbacks that proved unreliable across devices.
Motivation — Allama Iqbal
Offline
اقبال

80 authentic Iqbal couplets, tap-through, in proper Nastaliq script. Chosen deliberately over generic motivational quotes: Iqbal is the poet of self-belief in Pakistani education, and a student who reads خودی کو کر بلند اتنا feels something a translated productivity slogan cannot reach.

The hard part: authenticity. Sourced from Iqbal Academy and Rekhta rather than assembled from memory, then rendered in the correct Nastaliq typeface — not a fallback Arabic font, which looks wrong to any Urdu reader.

Practice & memory

Flashcards with spaced repetition
Offline

An FSRS-based review system that schedules each card for the moment you are about to forget it. Fully offline.

The hard part: a card you just failed must come back tomorrow, not in two months. Failing a mature card resets it to a short relearning interval regardless of how well you knew it before — an earlier version left just-failed cards scheduled 60 days out.
Theorem Dojo
Offline
مسئلہ ڈوجو

An interactive proof puzzle covering 10 PCTB geometry theorems. The student reads the setup, then arranges shuffled statement-and-reason steps into a valid proof, and gets per-step feedback.

The hard part: targeting. This exists because Question 9 on the Maths paper is a compulsory 8-mark theorem proof — a large, predictable block of marks that rewards drilling. Generic study apps have no way to know that.

Progress

Readiness & predicted grade
Offline
تیاری

Per-subject readiness scores, an overall predicted grade band, and an exam-day risk list of the chapters most likely to cost marks.

The hard part: ranking risk honestly. The list is sorted by marks at risk, not marks secured — otherwise low-weight subjects dominate the list and genuinely dangerous heavy chapters get hidden behind them.
Streaks & attention feedback
Offline

Daily streak tracking, plus a genuine feedback loop: Focus Guard measures how long the student's concentration actually holds, and feeds that back into the plan engine so it stops prescribing 45-minute blocks to someone whose attention breaks at 15.

The hard part: streak credit follows when work was completed, not when it was scheduled — otherwise studying ahead silently stripped the student's streak.

Your data, your control

Cloud backup
Optional
کلاؤڈ

Optional account-based backup to Supabase, so a lost or replaced phone does not mean a lost year. Backs up automatically after study, when the app closes, and on a regular heartbeat — plus a manual "Back up now" button. Also works as a plain file export/import with no account at all.

The hard part: never destroying a good backup. Four independent safeguards stop a fresh install from overwriting real data: a reinstall wipes the session, automatic backup starts off and only a deliberate action enables it, the app refuses to upload when there is no profile, and every upload carries a version number so an out-of-date phone is rejected rather than allowed to clobber newer work.
Settings & study profile
Offline

Edit name, class, group and board at any time. Toggle haptics, Focus Guard, spoken cues and voice selection. Includes read-only diagnostics showing AI key count and stored data counts.

The hard part: destructive actions. Changing class or group necessarily rebuilds the plan, so it is gated behind a confirmation naming exactly how many completed sessions would be lost — it previously fired on a single tap.
06
Engineering Rigour
معیار

A study plan is not a feature you can ship "mostly working". If the engine is wrong, a student studies the wrong thing for four months and finds out on exam day.

989
automated assertions, run before every build
6
independent test suites
20.7k
lines of TypeScript across 77 files
3
timezones every date test must pass in
Plan-engine invariants Every rule the engine promises — daily limits never exceeded, no session too short, subjects properly varied, every chapter covered — is asserted, across all six class × group combinations and every study-time option.
Day-by-day simulation Five different student behaviours are simulated across an entire exam runway, with every invariant re-checked after every simulated day. This is how "what if a student studies ahead for two weeks then stops" gets answered before a real student finds out.
Hostile-input testing Backup restore is tested against deliberately corrupted and malicious files. Untrusted data never reaches the app's state — every field is rebuilt from validated values.
Timezone correctness Dates are handled in local time, never UTC — tested in Karachi, and in extreme positive and negative offsets. An earlier UTC bug credited a 1 a.m. study session to the previous day.
Privacy — a hard constraint, not a policy page

Focus Guard is off by default and must be switched on deliberately. When running, no image is ever stored, written to disk, or transmitted — the app only ever receives about six numbers per reading (head angles, eye-open likelihood, a box size). There is no code path in the app capable of doing otherwise. A restored backup can never silently switch a camera on.

07
What We Don't Claim
دیانت

Every project of this size has edges. Naming them is part of the engineering, not an admission against it.

AI features need internet

Ustaad, quizzes, grading and note-scanning require a connection. Everything else — the plan, flashcards, Focus Guard, Theorem Dojo, readiness, Breathe, Iqbal — works fully offline. That split was deliberate, so a power cut costs the student four features rather than the app.

Face detection is a vendor model

Focus Guard uses Google's on-device detector. Google publishes no fairness data for it, and we can't alter the model. So the app is built to abstain rather than guess: when it can't get a clean read it says so, that time is excluded from scoring rather than counted against the student, and the message stays instructive instead of accusing.

Curriculum data is dated

Chapter weights come from the 2026 pairing schemes. Boards revise these. Where evidence was thin, the data says so in its own comments rather than presenting a guess as fact.

Readiness is an estimate

The predicted grade band is a planning signal built from coverage and quiz performance — useful for deciding what to study next, not a forecast of an actual board result.

On how this was built

Manzil was built with AI as a working partner — an approach the app discloses openly in its own Settings screen. Every architectural decision, every threshold, and every piece of curriculum data was reviewed, tested and defended against real code. The 989-assertion test suite exists precisely because "it looked right" is not evidence.

خودی کو کر بلند اتنا کہ ہر تقدیر سے پہلے
خدا بندے سے خود پوچھے بتا تیری رضا کیا ہے

Manzil means destination — named for what the student is walking toward, not for the app.

08
The Bench
تعمیر

Manzil was not built with "an AI". It was built with nine frontier models from three competing laboratories, assigned by strength and set against each other — because a model reviewing its own output is not review.

Anthropic · Claude
Architecture & Implementation
Fable 5
The frontier of the Claude 5 generation. Reserved for work where being almost right is worthless — the plan engine's invariants, the two-axis AI fallback, and thresholds that had to be derived rather than tuned by trial.
Opus 5
Anthropic's most capable production model and the project's primary engineer — the study algorithm, the AI resilience layer, Focus Guard's state machine, and every full-codebase audit. Nine commits carry its signature.
Opus 4.8
Adversarial stress-testing and the Gemini vision pipeline — used specifically to attack finished work and find what the builder had missed.
Sonnet 5
High-throughput implementation and live-device debugging, including the native face-detection fix that pure logic tests were structurally blind to.
Sonnet 4.6
Sustained feature build-out across the cloud-backup and settings surfaces.
Google · Gemini
Parallel Verification Teams
3.1 Pro
Google's deep-reasoning tier, run as a verification subagent team — parallel researchers checking curriculum claims against primary sources, so no chapter weight rested on one model's confidence.
3.6 Flash
The second verification team, cross-checking the same syllabus from independent sources — agreement across two labs was the bar for accepting a fact.
3.5 Flash
Also the model that ships inside Manzil, powering Ustaad, grading and quizzes — so it was validated as both a build tool and a runtime dependency.
OpenAI
Independent Audit
5.6 Terra
An outside auditor — a third lab with no stake in decisions the other two had made, reading the codebase cold to catch what shared assumptions hid.
This is why the 989-assertion test suite exists. Every model here can write code that looks correct; none can be trusted to certify its own. Real bugs — a plan engine stacking three identical subjects, a race showing a false "backed up" message, a face detector silently rejecting visible students — were each found by one model auditing another's work, then proven by a test that fails without the fix.
